pages.name: Direction
pages.title: Direction — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: How directors turn a script into a point of view, through blocking, lenses, performance and restraint.
pages.mf: A director’s vision is the thousand small answers to one question: what should the audience feel, and when?
notes: The dolly zoom
Hitchcock’s Vertigo (1958) pulled the camera back while zooming in, bending space so a character’s dizziness becomes the audience’s.
Hiding the monster
When the mechanical shark kept failing, Spielberg showed it as little as possible in Jaws. The suspense worked better than the effect would have.
Many cameras, one take
Kurosawa filmed the battles in Seven Samurai with several cameras at once, capturing chaos that could not be repeated.
Obsessive retakes
Kubrick demanded repeated takes. The bat scene in The Shining is widely reported at 127, a recognised record.
stats: reported takes for one scene in The Shining
the year Vertigo introduced the dolly zoom
frames a second, each one a decision
questions behind every shot: where, why, how
story: Directors work in layers. First comes the script, then the visual plan: storyboards, shot lists and rehearsals that decide where each camera will stand.
On set, blocking decides how actors move through space. A step toward the camera or a pause in a doorway can say more than a page of dialogue.
gloss: Planned movement of actors and camera.
Extra angles shot so editors have choices.
The director’s ordered plan of shots.

pages.name: Camera movements
pages.title: Camera movements — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Dolly, pan, tilt, crane, whip pan and handheld: what each movement does to the viewer, with a live camera to play with.
pages.mq: Dolly ✦ Pan ✦ Tilt ✦ Crane ✦ Whip pan ✦ Handheld ✦
pages.mf: A camera move is a decision about who is in control: the character, the audience or the filmmaker.
notes: Pan and tilt
The camera pivots on a fixed point, turning left-right or up-down, like a head turning to look.
Dolly and truck
The whole camera travels on wheels or track. Near things move faster than far things, so the move reveals real depth.
Crane and jib
A boom lifts the camera through space for rising reveals, from a face to the whole city around it.
Handheld
Operators carry the camera by hand to add urgency and instability, common in war films and documentaries.
stats: dolly zoom debuts in Vertigo
Steadicam makes smooth handheld possible
minutes of unbroken movement in Russian Ark
degrees in a full orbit around a subject
story: Choose a move by asking what the audience should feel. A slow push in builds intimacy or dread, a pull back reveals isolation, and a rising crane gives a sense of scale.
Planning matters as much as the move itself. Tracks must be levelled and laid, focus pullers rehearse distances, and actors hit marks so the shot lands once, smoothly.
gloss: Wheeled platform that moves the camera.
Raising or lowering the camera vertically.
Very fast pan that blurs the image.
pages.scope: The lens opens onto a moving world

pages.name: Lenses & framing
pages.title: Lenses & framing — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Shot sizes, focal length, depth of field and composition, with a lens you can adjust yourself.
pages.mq: Wide ✦ Close-up ✦ Focal length ✦ Depth of field ✦ Composition ✦
pages.mf: A lens is a choice about distance: how near we feel to a character, and how much of their world we see.
notes: Shot sizes
From extreme wide to extreme close-up, shot size controls how close we feel to a character.
Focal length
Wide lenses stretch space and exaggerate depth; telephoto lenses compress distance and flatten it.
Depth of field
Shallow focus isolates a subject; deep focus keeps near and far sharp, as in Citizen Kane (1941).
Thirds and the 180° line
Off-centre subjects feel natural, and staying on one side of an imaginary line keeps screen direction clear.
stats: Citizen Kane’s deep-focus cinematography
degree rule keeps screen direction clear
cells in the rule-of-thirds grid
mm, a classic portrait telephoto lens
story: Lenses change emotion without changing the actor. A wide lens close to a face feels distorted and anxious, while a long lens from far away feels observed and cool.
Composition guides the eye before anyone notices. Leading lines, foreground frames and empty space all tell the audience where to look and how to feel about it.
gloss: Squeezed lenses giving a wide frame.
pages.scope: Aspect ratio is a lens choice too

pages.name: Light & colour
pages.title: Light & colour — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: High-key, low-key, Rembrandt and backlight, plus colour temperature, with a light rig you can drag.
pages.mq: Key ✦ Fill ✦ Backlight ✦ Colour temperature ✦ Practicals ✦
pages.mf: Light is the first actor on set: it decides mood before anyone speaks.
notes: High-key and low-key
High-key is bright and even, common in comedy; low-key is contrasty with deep shadows, the look of film noir.
Rembrandt lighting
A small triangle of light on the shadowed cheek, borrowed from the painter, gives faces depth and drama.
Colour temperature
Daylight reads cool and blue, tungsten reads warm and orange; filmmakers mix them to separate worlds.
Practical lights
Lamps and neon visible in the frame also light the scene, making rooms feel lived in.
stats: lights in the classic three-point setup
kelvin, a standard daylight colour temperature
kelvin, standard tungsten warmth
O Brother is the first fully digitally graded feature
story: Start with one light. Place the key where the sun or a window would be, then ask what the shadows are doing. Fill, backlight and colour are added only to serve that first idea.
Cinematographers often light for the emotional truth of a scene rather than strict realism, letting a window glow brighter than it should so a face can glow with it.
gloss: Cutout that shapes light into patterns.

pages.name: Editing & sound
pages.title: Editing & sound — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Cut types, rhythm, montage and sound design, with a transition lab where you can try every cut.
pages.mq: Hard cut ✦ Match cut ✦ L-cut ✦ Montage ✦ Foley ✦ Mix ✦
pages.mf: Editing is where the film is finally made: the same footage can become a different story.
notes: The match cut
2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) cuts from a thrown bone to an orbiting satellite, linking millions of years in one edit.
The hard cut
The default: an instant switch that, when done well, the audience never notices.
L-cut and J-cut
Sound from the next scene begins before the picture changes, or lingers after, making cuts feel smooth.
Sound design
Silence, room tone and one Foley detail can frighten more than music, because the audience fills in the rest.
stats: 2001’s bone-to-satellite match cut
The Great Train Robbery and early continuity editing
frames in one second of film
channels in a 7.1 cinema mix
story: Rhythm is the editor’s first tool. Short shots speed the pulse, long shots let a moment breathe, and a well-placed pause can feel louder than any explosion.
Sound carries half the experience. Dialogue, effects, music and silence are balanced in the final mix, often in a room built to sound like a cinema.
gloss: Series of shots compressed into meaning.
Silent recording of a location’s ambience.

pages.name: Stunts & action
pages.title: Stunts & action — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Stunt coordination, wire work, practical effects and the people who make danger look effortless.
pages.mq: Wire work ✦ Falls ✦ Car chases ✦ Fight design ✦ Pyrotechnics ✦ Safety ✦
pages.mf: A stunt is choreography with consequences, designed so the audience feels the danger and the crew feels none of it.
notes: Keaton’s falling house
In Steamboat Bill, Jr. (1928), a heavy house front fell around Buster Keaton, who stood on a marked spot with an open window just inches either side.
Real vehicles, real impact
Mad Max: Fury Road (2015) built working vehicles and filmed most of its chases in camera, using digital effects mainly to enhance them.
The cliff jump
For Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning, Tom Cruise reportedly practised thousands of motorcycle jumps and hundreds of skydives first.
Rigs and safety
Teams plan with wires, air rams, ratchets, padded landings and safety crews, so the danger lives on screen and not on set.
stats: year of Keaton’s house-front stunt
Fury Road, built around practical action
first planned Oscars for stunt design
parts to every gag: plan, rehearse, shoot
story: Every stunt begins on paper. The coordinator and director agree what the audience must see, then design the safest way to deliver it.
Rehearsal is slow on purpose. Speeds, distances, cameras and medics are locked before the first take, so spontaneity belongs to the performance, not the risk.
gloss: Small charge that simulates a bullet hit.
Compressed-air device that throws a performer.
pages.scope: Widescreen action needs room to land

pages.name: Behind the scenes
pages.title: Behind the scenes — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: The crew, the set and the process between “action” and the finished film.
pages.mq: Call sheet ✦ Slate ✦ Gaffers ✦ Continuity ✦ Foley ✦ Wrap ✦
pages.mf: Behind every effortless scene is a crowd: cameras, cables, schedules, weather and people solving small problems all day.
notes: The call sheet
Every shooting day starts with a call sheet: who is needed, where, when, and which scenes will be filmed.
Shot out of order
Films are usually shot by location and schedule, not story order, so a script supervisor tracks continuity down to props and hair.
The slate
The clapperboard marks scene and take, and gives editors a visual and audio sync point for picture and sound.
Foley and the mix
After the shoot, Foley artists recreate footsteps, cloth and props in a studio, then sound teams blend them with dialogue and music.
stats: stages: pre-production, shoot, post-production
hours in a typical long shooting day
crew on larger productions, often far more
slate for every single take
story: A shoot day runs on a tight clock. The assistant director keeps the schedule while departments prepare the next set as the crew shoots the current one.
Lighting changes take longer than performances. One new camera angle can mean re-lighting the room, which is why coverage is planned carefully.
gloss: Head of the electrical and lighting crew.
Crew who build rigs and move camera supports.
The end of filming for the day or the film.

pages.name: Filmmaking methods
pages.title: Filmmaking methods — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Lighting, camera movement, editing, colour and virtual production, explained plainly.
pages.mq: Lighting ✦ Lenses ✦ Editing ✦ Colour ✦ Sound ✦ Virtual production ✦
pages.mf: Method is how a feeling becomes repeatable: a lens, a light, a cut, a sound, placed with intent.
notes: Three-point lighting
A key light shapes the face, a fill softens shadows and a backlight separates the subject from the background.
The Steadicam
Garrett Brown’s Steadicam let operators glide smoothly on foot. It debuted in Bound for Glory (1976) and soon defined Rocky and The Shining.
The Kuleshov effect
Early Soviet experiments showed the same face reads differently depending on the shot beside it, proving editing creates meaning.
LED volumes
Virtual production surrounds actors with real-time LED screens. The Mandalorian (2019) helped popularise the approach.
stats: frames a second, the sound-era standard
Steadicam’s feature debut
first fully digitally graded feature, O Brother, Where Art Thou?
The Mandalorian popularises LED volumes
story: Methods are shared tools, not rules. Directors and cinematographers borrow, bend and break them to serve a particular feeling.
Technology keeps changing the options, from film stock to digital sensors to LED stages, but the questions stay the same: where do we look, and what do we feel?
gloss: Main source that shapes the subject.
Scanning and grading film as digital data.

pages.name: VFX & virtual sets
pages.title: VFX & virtual sets — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Practical effects, miniatures, motion capture and LED stages, with a virtual set that follows your pointer.
pages.mq: Practical ✦ Miniatures ✦ Motion capture ✦ CGI ✦ LED volumes ✦
pages.mf: The best effect is the one built from real light, even when part of it is pixels.
notes: Practical first
Models, makeup, animatronics and pyrotechnics still ground effects in real light and texture.
Miniatures and mattes
Before CG, painted glass and scale models extended sets; Star Wars (1977) pushed motion-control miniatures forward.
Motion capture
Actors’ movements are recorded and applied to digital characters, as with Gollum in The Lord of the Rings.
LED volumes
Screens track the camera so backgrounds shift in correct perspective, giving actors real light and context.
stats: Star Wars and the motion-control era
Tron’s early computer-generated imagery
Gollum’s motion-capture performance debuts
The Mandalorian popularises LED volumes
story: Visual effects start long before post-production. Supervisors join early to plan which shots need blue screens, which need real sets, and which can be solved with clever camera angles.
Virtual production changes the order of work. Environments are built first, the camera moves inside them on set, and many decisions once made months later are made in the room.
gloss: Footage that effects are added to.

pages.name: Cinema facts
pages.title: Cinema facts — Frame Atlas
pages.intro: Origin stories, firsts, records and oddities from film history, in short, checkable pieces.
pages.mq: Firsts ✦ Records ✦ Sound ✦ Colour ✦ Oddities ✦ History ✦
pages.mf: Cinema is barely a century and a quarter old, and it has already invented a new grammar for how we see.
notes: First public screening
The Lumière brothers held the first paid public film screening in Paris on 28 December 1895.
Sound arrives
The Jazz Singer (1927) made synchronised sound a business, and 24 frames a second became the standard.
One shot, 96 minutes
Russian Ark (2002) is a single unbroken Steadicam shot through the Hermitage, running about 96 minutes.
The Wilhelm scream
A stock scream first heard in Distant Drums (1951) has since turned up in countless films as an in-joke.
stats: first public screening, Paris
The Jazz Singer and the sound era
minutes in Russian Ark’s single shot
first appearance of the Wilhelm scream
story: Film history moves in jumps: a new machine arrives, audiences learn a new habit, and storytellers invent a grammar to match it.
Many early rules were accidents of technology. Even 24 frames per second came from sound and cost, not from any perfect number.
